chapters.title: INTRODUCTION
chapters.text_markdown:
## INTRODUCTION.
If a block of wood or stone is cut in the shape represented in Fig. 1, it will have *six flat faces*. Each face of the block is called a surface; and if the faces are made smooth by polishing, so that, when a straight edge is applied to any one of them, the straight edge in every part will touch the surface, the faces are called **plane surfaces**, or **planes**.
**.** The intersectionof any two of these surfaces is called a **line**. **.** The intersection of any three of these lines is called a **point**.
The block extends in three principal directions:
From left to right, $A$ to $B$. From front to back, $A$ to $C$. From top to bottom, $A$ to $D$.
These are called the **dimensions**of the block, and are named in the order given, **length**, **breadth** (or *width*), and **thickness** (*height* or *depth*).
A **solid**, in common language, is a limited portion of space *filled with matter*; but in Geometry we have nothing to do with *the matter* of which a body is composed; we study simply its *shape* and *size*; that is, we regard a solid as a limited portion of space which may be occupied by a physical body, or marked out in some other way. Hence, *A geometrical solidis a limited portion of space.*
The surfaceof a solid is simply the boundary of the solid, that which separates it from surrounding space. The surface is no part of a solid and has no thickness. Hence, *A surface has only two dimensions, length and breadth.*
A lineis simply a boundary of a surface, or the intersection of two surfaces. Since the surfaces have no thickness, a line has no thickness. Moreover, a line is no part of a surface and has no width. Hence, *A line has only one dimension, length.*
A pointis simply the extremity of a line, or the intersection of two lines. A point, therefore, has no thickness, width, or length; therefore, no magnitude. Hence, *A point has no dimension, but denotes position simply.*
It must be distinctly understood at the outset that the points, lines, surfaces, and solids of Geometry are *purely ideal*, though they are represented to the eye in a material way. Lines, for example, drawn on paper or on the blackboard, will have some width and some thickness, and will so far fail of being *true lines*; yet, when they are used to help the mind in reasoning, it is assumed that they represent true lines, without breadth and without thickness.
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/012aaZ10.png)
A point is *represented* to the eye by a fine dot, and named by a letter, as $A$ (Fig. 2). A line is named by two letters, placed one at each end, as $BF$. A surfaceis represented and named by the lines which bound it, as $BCDF$. A solidis represented by the faces which bound it.
**.** A point in space may be considered by itself, without reference to a line. **.** If a point moves in space, its path is a line. This line may be considered apart from the idea of a surface. **.** If a line moves in space, it generates, in general, a surface. A surface can then be considered apart from the idea of a solid.
If a surface moves in space, it generates, in general, a solid. ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/012bbZ14.png) Thus, let the upright surface $ABCD$ (Fig. 3) move to the right to the position $EFGH$, the points $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ generating the lines $AE$, $BF$, $CG$, and $DH$, respectively. The lines $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$ will generate the surfaces $AF$. $BG$, $CH$, and $DE$, respectively. The surface $ABCD$ will generate the solid $AG$.
**.** **Geometry** is the science which treats of *position, form*, and *magnitude*. **.** A **geometrical figure** is a combination of points, lines, surfaces, or solids.
**Plane Geometry** treats of figures all points of which are in the same plane. **Solid Geometry** treats of figures all points of which are not in the same plane.
## GENERAL TERMS.
A **proof** is a course of reasoning by which the truth or falsity of any statement is logically established.
An **axiom**is a statement admitted to be true without proof.
A **theorem** is a statement to be proved.
A **construction**is the representation of a required figure by means of points and lines.
A **postulate** is a construction admitted to be possible.
A **problem** is a construction to be made so that it shall satisfy certain given conditions.
A **proposition** is an axiom, a theorem, a postulate, or a problem.
A **corollary** is a truth that is easily deduced from known truths.
A **scholium** is a remark upon some particular feature of a proposition.
The **solution of a problem** consists of four parts: 1\. The *analysis*, or course of thought by which the construction of the required figure is discovered. 2\. The *construction* of the figure with the aid of ruler and compasses. 3\. The *proof* that the figure satisfies all the conditions. 4\. The *discussion* of the limitations, if any, within which the solution is possible.
A theorem consists of two parts: the **hypothesis**, or that which is assumed; and the **conclusion**, or that which is asserted to follow from the hypothesis.
The **contradictory** of a theoremis a theorem which must be true if the given theorem is false, and must be false if the given theorem is true. Thus,\ A theorem: If $A$ is $B$, then $C$ is $D$.\ Its contradictory: If $A$ is $B$, then $C$ is not $D$.
The **opposite** of a theorem is obtained by making *both the hypothesis and the conclusion negative*. Thus,\ A theorem: If $A$ is $B$, then $C$ is $D$.\ Its opposite: If $A$ is not $B$, then $C$ is not $D$.
The **converse**of a theorem is obtained by *interchanging the hypothesis and conclusion*. Thus,\ A theorem: If $A$ is $B$, then $C$ is $D$.\ Its converse: If $C$ is $D$, then $A$ is $B$.
The converse of a truth is not *necessarily* true. Thus, Every horse is a quadruped is true, but the converse, Every quad­ru­ped is a horse, is not true.
*If a direct proposition and its opposite are true, the converse proposition is true; and if a direct proposition and its converse are true, the opposite proposition is true*. Thus, if it were true that 1\. If an animal is a horse, the animal is a quadruped; 2\. If an animal is not a horse, the animal is not a quadruped;\ it would follow that 3\. If an animal is a quadruped, the animal is a horse. Moreover, if 1 and 3 were true, then 2 would be true.
## **.**GENERAL AXIOMS. 1\. Magnitudes which are equal to the same magnitude, or equal magnitudes, are equal to each other. 2\. If equals are added to equals, the sums are equal. 3\. If equals are taken from equals, the remainders are equal. 4\. If equals are added to unequals, the sums are unequal in the same order; if unequals are added to unequals in the same order, the sums are unequal in that order. 5\. If equals are taken from unequals, the remainders are unequal in the same order; if unequals are taken from equals, the remainders are unequal in the reverse order. 6\. The doubles of the same magnitude, or of equal magnitudes are equal; and the doubles of unequals are unequal. 7\. The halves of the same magnitude, or of equal magnitudes are equal; and the halves of unequals are unequal. 8\. The whole is greater than any of its parts. 9\. The whole is equal to the sum of all its parts. ## **.**SYMBOLS AND ABBREVIATIONS. -------------- ----------------------------------- -------- ---------------- $>$ is (or are) greater than. Def. definition. $<$ is (or are) less than. Ax. axiom. $\Bumpeq$ is (or are) equivalent to. Hyp. hypothesis. $\therefore$ therefore. Cor. corollary. $\perp$ perpendicular. Scho. scholium. $\perp_s$ perpendiculars. Ex. exercise. $\parallel$ parallel.$\parallel_s$ parallels. Adj. adjacent. $\angle$ angle.$\angle_s$ angles. Iden. identical. $\triangle$ triangle.$\triangle_s$ triangles. Const. construction. $\Par$ parallelogram. Sup. supplementary. $\Par_s$ parallelograms. Ext. exterior. $\odot$ circle.$\odot_s$ circles. Int. interior. rt. right.st. straight. Alt. alternate. -------------- ----------------------------------- -------- ---------------- q.e.d. stands for quod erat demonstrandum, *which was to be proved*. q.e.f. stands for quod erat faciendum, *which was to be done.* The signs $+$, $-$, $×$, $\div$, $=$, have the same meaning as in Algebra. PLANE GEOMETRY.

chapters.title: RECTILINEAR FIGURES
chapters.text_markdown:
# BOOK I. RECTILINEAR FIGURES. ## DEFINITIONS. ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/016aaZ37.png)
A **straight line** is a line such that any part of it, however placed on any other part, will lie wholly in that part if its extremities lie in that part, as $AB$.
A **curved line** is a line no part of which is straight, as $CD$.
A **broken line** is made up of different straight lines, as $EF$.
Note. A straight line is often called simply a *line*.
A **plane surface**, or a **plane**, is a surface in which, if any two points are taken, the straight line joining these points lies wholly in the surface.
A **curved surface**is a surface no part of which is plane.
A **plane figure** is a figure all points of which are in the same plane.
Plane figures which are bounded by straight lines are called **rectilinear** figures; by curved lines, **curvilinear** figures.
Figures that have the *same shape* are called **similar**. Figures that have the *same size but not the same shape* are called **equivalent**. Figures that have the *same shape and the same size* are called **equal**or **congruent**.
## THE STRAIGHT LINE. **.** **Postulate.** A straight line can be drawn from one point to another. **.** **Postulate.** A straight line can be produced indefinitely. **.** **Axiom.**[^1] *Only one straight line can be drawn from one point to another.* Hence, two points *determine* a straight line. **.** Cor. 1. 
Two straight lines which have two points in common coincide and form but one line.
**.** Cor. 2. 
Two straight lines can intersect in only one point.
For if they had two points common, they would coincide and not intersect. Hence, two intersecting lines *determine* a point. **.** **Axiom. ***A straight line is the shortest line that can be drawn from one point to another.* **.** Def. The **distance**between two points is the length of the straight line that joins them. **.** A straight line determined by two points may be considered as prolonged indefinitely. **.** If only the part of the line between two fixed points is considered, this part is called a **segment** of the line. **.** For brevity, we say "the line $AB$," to designate a segment of a line limited by the points $A$ and $B$. **.** If a line is considered as extending from a fixed point, this point is called the **origin** of the line. ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/018aaZ55.png)
If any point, $C$, is taken in a given straight line, $AB$, the two parts $CA$ and $CB$ are said to have *opposite directions* from the point $C$ (Fig. 5). Every straight line, as $AB$, may be considered as extending in either of two opposite directions, namely, from $A$ towards $B$, which is expressed by $AB$, and read segment $AB$; and from $B$ towards $A$, which is expressed by $BA$, and read segment $BA$.
If the magnitude of a given line is changed, it becomes longer or shorter. Thus (Fig. 5), by prolonging $AC$ to $B$ we add $CB$ to $AC$, and $AB = AC+CB$. By diminishing $AB$ to $C$, we subtract $CB$ from $AB$, and $AC = AB-CB$. If a given line increases so that it is prolonged by its own magnitude several times in succession, the line is *multiplied*, and the resulting line is called a *multiple* of the given line. ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/018bbZ56.png) Thus (Fig. 6), if $AB = BC = CD = DE$, then $AC = 2AB$, $AD = 3AB$, and $AE = 4AB$. Hence, *Lines of given length may be added and subtracted; they may also be multiplied by a number.*
## THE PLANE ANGLE. ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/018ccZ57.png)
The *opening* between two straight lines drawn from the same point is called a **plane angle**. The two lines, $ED$ and $EF$, are called the **sides**, and $E$, the point of meeting, is called the **vertex** of the angle. The size of an angle depends upon the *extent of opening* of its sides, and not upon the length of its sides.
If there is but one angle at a given vertex, the angle is designated by a capital letter placed at the vertex, and is read by simply naming the letter. ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/019aaZ58.png)![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/019bbZ58.png) If two or more angles have the same vertex, each angle is designated by three letters, and is read by naming the three letters, the one at the vertex between the others. Thus, $DAC$ (Fig. 8) is the angle formed by the sides $AD$ and $AC$. An angle is often designated by placing a small *italic* letter between the sides and near the vertex, as in Fig. 9.
**Postulate of Superposition.**Any figure may be moved from one place to another without altering its size or shape.
The **test of equality** of two geometrical magnitudes is that they may be made to coincide throughout their whole extent. Thus, Two straight lines are equal, if they can be placed one upon the other so that the points at their extremities coincide. Two angles are equal, if they can be placed one upon the other so that their vertices coincide and their sides coincide, each with each.
A line or plane that divides a geometric magnitude into *two equal parts* is called the **bisector**of the magnitude. If the angles $BAD$ and $CAD$ (Fig. 8) are equal, $AD$ *bisects* the angle $BAC$.
Two angles are called **adjacent angles**when they have the same vertex and a common side between them; as the angles $BOD$ and $AOD$ (Fig. 10).
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/019ccZ62.png)![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/020aaZ63.png)
When one straight line meets another straight line and makes the *adjacent angles equal*, each of these angles is called a **right angle**; as angles $DCA$ and $DCB$ (Fig. 11).
A **perpendicular** to a straight line is a straight line that makes a right angle with it. Thus, if the angle $DCA$ (Fig. 11) is a right angle, $DC$ is perpendicular to $AB$, and $AB$ is perpendicular to $DC$.
The point (as $C$, Fig. 11) where a perpendicular meets another line is called the **foot** of the perpendicular.
When the sides of an angle extend in opposite directions, so as to be in the same straight line, the angle is called a **straight angle**. ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/020bbZ66.png) Thus, the angle formed at $C$ (Fig. 12) with its sides $CA$ and $CB$ extending in opposite directions from $C$ is a straight angle.
**.** Cor. 
A right angle is half a straight angle.
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/020ccZ68.png)![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/020ddZ69.png)
An angle less than a right angle is called an **acute angle**; as, angle $A$ (Fig. 13).
An angle greater than a right angle and less than a straight angle is called an **obtuse angle**; as, angle $AOD$ (Fig. 14).
An angle greater than a straight angle and less than two straight angles is called a **reflex angle**; as, angle $DOA$, indicated by the dotted line (Fig. 14).
Angles that are neither right nor straight angles are called **oblique angles**; and intersecting lines that are not perpendicular to each other are called **oblique lines**.
### EXTENSION OF THE MEANING OF ANGLES. ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/021aaZ72.png)
Suppose the straight line $OC$ (Fig. 15) to move in the plane of the paper from coincidence with $OA$, about the point $O$ as a pivot, to the position $OC$; then the line $OC$ describes or generates *the angle $AOC$*, and the magnitude of the angle $AOC$ depends upon the *amount of rotation* of the line from the position $OA$ to the position $OC$. If the rotating line moves from the position $OA$ to the position $OB$, *perpendicular* to $OA$, it generates the right angle $AOB$; if it moves to the position $OD$, it generates the obtuse angle $AOD$; if it moves to the position $OA'$, it generates the straight angle $AOA'$; if it moves to the position $OB'$ it generates the reflex angle $AOB'$, indicated by the dotted line; and if it moves to the position $OA$ again, it generates two straight angles. Hence,
*The angular magnitude about a point in a plane is equal to two straight angles, or four right angles; and the angular magnitude about a point on one side of a straight line drawn through the point is equal to a straight angle, or two right angles.*
The whole angular magnitude about a point in a plane is called a **perigon**; and two angles whose sum is a perigon are called **conjugate angles**.
Note. This *extension of the meaning of angles* is necessary in the applications of Geometry, as in Trigonometry, Mechanics, etc.
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/022aaZ75.png) ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/022bbZ76.png) ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/022ccZ77.png)
When two angles have the same vertex, and the sides of the one are prolongations of the sides of the other, they are called **vertical angles**; as, angles $a$ and $b$, $c$ and $d$ (Fig. 16).
Two angles are called **complementary**when their sum is equal to a right angle; and each is called the *complement*of the other; as, angles $DOB$ and $DOC$ (Fig. 17).
Two angles are called **supplementary**when their sum is equal to a straight angle; and each is called the *supplement* of the other; as, angles $DOB$ and $DOA$ (Fig. 18).
### UNIT OF ANGLES.
By adopting a suitable unit for measuring angles we are able to express the magnitudes of angles by numbers. If we suppose $OC$ (Fig. 15) to turn about $O$ from coincidence with $OA$ until it makes *one three hundred sixtieth* of a revolution, it generates an angle at $O$, which is taken as the unit for measuring angles. This unit is called a *degree*. The degree is subdivided into sixty equal parts, called *minutes*, and the minute into sixty equal parts, called *seconds*. Degrees, minutes, and seconds are denoted by symbols. Thus, $5$ degrees $13$ minutes $12$ seconds is written $5°\ 13'\ 12''$. A right angle is generated when $OC$ has made *one fourth* of a revolution and contains $90°$; a straight angle, when $OC$ has made *half* of a revolution and contains $180°$; and a perigon, when $OC$ has made a complete revolution and contains $360°$.
Note. The natural angular unit is one complete revolution. But this unit would require us to express the values of most angles by fractions. The advantage of using the degree as the unit consists in its convenient size, and in the fact that $360$ is divisible by so many different integral numbers.
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/023aaZ79.png)
By the method of superposition we are able to compare magnitudes of the same kind. Suppose we have two angles, $ABC$ and $DEF$ (Fig. 19). Let the side $ED$ be placed on the side $BA$, so that the vertex $E$ shall fall on $B$; then, if the side $EF$ falls on $BC$, the angle $DEF$ equals the angle $ABC$; if the side $EF$ falls between $BC$ and $BA$ in the position shown by the dotted line $BG$, the angle $DEF$ is less than the angle $ABC$; but if the side $EF$ falls in the position shown by the dotted line $BH$, the angle $DEF$ is greater than the angle $ABC$.
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/023bcZ80.png)
If we have the angles $ABC$ and $DEF$ (Fig. 20), and place the vertex $E$ on $B$ and the side $ED$ on $BC$, so that the angle $DEF$ takes the position $CBH$, the angles $DEF$ and $ABC$ will together be equal to the angle $ABH$. If the vertex $E$ is placed on $B$, and the side $ED$ on $BA$, so that the angle $DEF$ takes the position $ABF$, the angle $FBC$ will be the difference between the angles $ABC$ and $DEF$. If an angle is increased by its own magnitude two or more times in succession, the angle is *multiplied* by a number. Thus, if the angles $ABM$, $MBC$, $CBP$, $PBD$ (Fig. 21) are all equal, the angle $ABD$ is $4$ times the angle $ABM$. Therefore, *Angles may be added and subtracted; they may also be multiplied by a number.*
## PERPENDICULAR AND OBLIQUE LINES. Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *All straight angles are equal.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/024aaZ81.png) **Let the angles $ACB$ and $DEF$ be any two straight angles.** *To prove that $\angle ACB = \angle DEF$*. **Proof.** Place the $\angle ACB$ on the $\angle DEF$, so that the vertex $C$ shall fall on the vertex $E$, and the side $CB$ on the side $EF$. Then $CA$ will fall on $ED$, *(because $ACB$ and $DEF$ are straight lines).* $\therefore \angle ACB = \angle DEF$. q.e.d. ◻
**.** Cor. 1. 
All right angles are equal.
 Ax. 7
Cor. 2. 
At a given point in a given line there can be but one perpendicular to the line.
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/024bbZ83.png) For, if there could be two $\perp_s$, we should have rt. $\angle_s$ of different magnitudes; but this is impossible, § 82.
**.** Cor. 3. 
The complements of the same angle or of equal angles are equal.
 Ax. 3 **.** Cor. 4. 
The supplements of the same angle or of equal angles are equal.
 Ax. 3
Note. The beginner must not forget that in Plane Geometry all the points of a figure are in the same plane. Without this restriction in Cor. 2, an indefinite number of perpendiculars can be erected at a given point in a given line.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *If two adjacent angles have their exterior sides in a straight line, these angles are supplementary.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/025aaZ86.png) **Let the exterior sides $OA$ and $OB$ of the adjacent angles $AOD$ and $BOD$ be in the straight line $AB$.** *To prove that $\angle_s AOD$ and $BOD$ are supplementary.* $AOB$ is a straight line. $\therefore \angle AOB$ is a st. $\angle$. $\angle AOD + \angle BOD =$ the st. $\angle AOB$. $\therefore$ the $\angle_s AOD$ and $BOD$ are supplementary. q.e.d. ◻
Def. Adjacent angles that are supplements of each other are called *supplementary-adjacent angles*. Since the angular magnitude about a point is neither increased nor diminished by the number of lines which radiate from the point, it follows that,
**.** Cor. 1. 
The sum of all the angles about a point in a plane is equal to a perigon, or two straight angles.
**.** Cor. 2. 
The sum of all the angles about a point in a plane, on the same side of a straight line passing through the point, is equal to a straight angle, or two right angles.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *Conversely: If two adjacent angles are supplementary, their exterior sides are in the same straight line.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/026aaZ90.png) **Let the adjacent angles $OCA$ and $OCB$ be supplementary.** *To prove that $AC$ and $CB$ are in the same straight line.* **Proof.** Suppose $CF$ to be in the same line with $AC$. $\angle_s OCA$ and $OCF$ are supplementary, *(if two adjacent angles have their exterior sides in a straight line, these angles are supplementary).* $\angle_s OCA$ and $OCB$ are supplementary. $\therefore \angle_s OCF$ and $OCB$ have the same supplement.  $\therefore \angle OCF$ $= \angle OCB$.  $\therefore CB$ and $CF$ coincide. $\therefore AC$ and $CB$ are in the same straight line. Since Propositions II. and III. are true, their opposites are true. Hence, § 33 ◻
**.** Cor. 1. 
If the exterior sides of two adjacent angles are not in a straight line, these angles are not supplementary.
**.** Cor. 2. 
If two adjacent angles are not supplementary, their exterior sides are not in the same straight line.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *If one straight line intersects another straight line, the vertical angles are equal.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/027aaZ93.png) **Let the lines $OP$ and $AB$ intersect at $C$.**  $\angle OCB$ $= \angle ACP$.  $\angle OCA$ and $\angle OCB$ are supplementary. $\angle OCA$ and $\angle ACP$ are supplementary, *(if two adjacent angles have their exterior sides in a straight line, these angles are supplementary).* $\therefore \angle_s OCB$ and $ACP$ have the same supplement.  $\therefore \angle OCB$ $= \angle ACP$.   $\angle ACO$ $= \angle PCB$.  ◻
**.** Cor. 
If one of the four angles formed by the intersection of two straight lines is a right angle, the other three angles are right angles.
**Ex. **.** ** Find the complement and the supplement of an angle of $49°$. **Ex. **.** ** Find the number of degrees in an angle if it is double its complement; if it is one fourth of its complement. **Ex. **.** ** Find the number of degrees in an angle if it is double its supplement; if it is one third of its supplement. Proposition . Theorem
*Proof.* *Two straight lines drawn from a point in a perpendicular to a given line, cutting off on the given line equal segments from the foot of the perpendicular, are equal and make equal angles with the perpendicular.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/028aaZ95.png) **Let $CF$ be a perpendicular to the line $AB$, and $CE$ and $CK$ two straight lines cutting off on $AB$ equal segments $FE$ and $FK$ from $F$.** *To prove that $CE = CK$; and $\angle FCE = \angle FCK$.* **Proof.** Fold over $CFA$, on $CF$ as an axis, until it falls on the plane at the right of $CF$. $FA$ will fall along $FB$, *(since $\angle CFA = \angle CFB$, each being a rt. $\angle$, by hyp.).* Point $E$ will fall on point $K$, *(since $FE = FK$, by hyp.).*  $\therefore CE$ $= CK$,  *(their extremities being the same points);*  and $\angle FCE$ $= \angle FCK$,  *(since their vertices coincide, and their sides coincide, each with each).* q.e.d. ◻
**Ex. **.** ** Find the number of degrees in the angle included by the hands of a clock at $1$ o'clock. $3$ o'clock. $4$ o'clock. $6$ o'clock. Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *Only one perpendicular can be drawn to a given line from a given external point.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/029aaZ96.png) **Let $AB$ be the given line, $P$ the given external point, $PC$ a perpendicular to $AB$ from $P$, and $PD$ any other line from $P$ to $AB$.**  $PD$ is not $\perp$ to $AB$.  **Proof.** Produce $PC$ to $P'$, making $CP'$ equal to $PC$. Draw $DP'$. By construction, $PCP'$ is a straight line. $\therefore PDP'$ is not a straight line, *(only one straight line can be drawn from one point to another).* Hence, $\angle PDP'$ is not a straight angle. Since $PC$ is $\perp$ to $DC$, and $PC = CP'$, $AC$ is $\perp$ to $PP'$ at its middle point. $\therefore \angle PDC = \angle P'DC$, *(two straight lines from a point in a $\perp$ to a line, cutting off on the line equal segments from the foot of the $\perp$, make equal $\angle_s$ with the $\perp$)* Since $\angle PDP'$ is not a straight angle, $\angle PDC$, the half of $\angle PDP'$, is not a right angle. $\therefore PD$ is not $\perp$ to $AB$. ◻
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *The perpendicular is the shortest line that can be drawn to a straight line from an external point.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/030aaZ97.png) **Let $AB$ be the given straight line, $P$ the given point, $PC$ the perpendicular, and $PD$ any other line drawn from $P$ to $AB$.**  $PC$ $< PD$.  **Proof.** Produce $PC$ to $P'$, making $CP' = PC$. Draw $DP'$.  $PD$ $= DP'$,  *(two straight lines drawn from a point in a $\perp$ to a line, cutting off on the line equal segments from the foot of the $\perp$, are equal).*  $\therefore PD + DP'$ $= 2PD$,   $PC + CP'$ $= 2PC$.   $PC + CP'$ $< PD + DP'$.   $\therefore 2 PC$ $< 2 PD$.   $\therefore PC$ $< PD$.  q.e.d. ◻
**.** Cor. 
The shortest line that can be drawn from a point to a given line is perpendicular to the given line.
**.** Def. The **distance**of a point from a line is the length of the perpendicular from the point to the line. Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *The sum of two lines drawn from a point to the extremities of a straight line is greater than the sum of two other lines similarly drawn, but included by them.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/031aa100.png) **Let $CA$ and $CB$ be two lines drawn from the point $C$ to the extremities of the straight line $AB$. Let $OA$ and $OB$ be two lines similarly drawn, but included by $CA$ and $CB$.**  $CA + CB$ $> OA + OB$.  **Proof.** Produce $AO$ to meet the line $CB$ at $E$.  $CA + CE$ $> OA + OE$,   $BE + OE$ $> OB$,  *(a straight line is the shortest line from one point to another).* Add these inequalities, and we have  $CA + CE + BE + OE$ $> OA + OE + OB$.  Substitute for $CE + BE$ its equal $CB$, then  $CA + CB + OE$ $> OA + OE + OB$.  Take away $OE$ from each side of the inequality.  $CA + CB$ $> OA + OB$.  q.e.d. ◻
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *Of two straight lines drawn from the same point in a perpendicular to a given line, cutting off on the line unequal segments from the foot of the perpendicular, the more remote is the greater.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/032aa101.png) **Let $OC$ be perpendicular to $AB$, $OG$ and $OE$ two straight lines to $AB$, and $CE$ greater than $CG$.**  $OE$ $> OG$.  **Proof.** Take $CF$ equal to $CG$, and draw $OF$.  $OF$ $= OG$,  *(two straight lines drawn from a point in a $\perp$ to a line, cutting off on the line equal segments from the foot of the $\perp$, are equal).* Produce $OC$ to $D$, making $CD = OC$. Draw $ED$ and $FD$. $OE = ED$, and $OF = FD$.  $OE + ED$ $> OF + FD$,   $\therefore 2OE > 2OF$, $OE$ $> OF$, and $OE > OG$.  ◻
**.** Cor. 
Only two equal straight lines can be drawn from a point to a straight line; and of two unequal lines, the greater cuts off on the line the greater segment from the foot of the perpendicular.
## PARALLEL LINES. **.** Def. Two **parallel lines** are lines that lie in the same plane and cannot meet however far they are produced. Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *Two straight lines in the same plane perpendicular to the same straight line are parallel.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/033aa104.png) **Let $AB$ and $CD$ be perpendicular to $AC$.** *To prove that $AB$ and $CD$ are parallel.* **Proof.** If $AB$ and $CD$ are not parallel, they will meet if sufficiently prolonged; and we shall have two perpendicular lines from their point of meeting to the same straight line; but this is impossible, § 96 *(only one perpendicular can be drawn to a given line from a given external point).* $\therefore AB$ and $CD$ are parallel. ◻
**.** **Axiom. ***Through a given point only one straight line can be drawn parallel to a given straight line.*
Cor. 
Two straight lines in the same plane parallel to a third straight line are parallel to each other.
For if they could meet, we should have two straight lines from the point of meeting parallel to a straight line; but this is impossible. § 105
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *If a straight line is perpendicular to one of two parallel lines, it is perpendicular to the other also.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/034aa107.png) **Let $AB$ and $EF$ be two parallel lines, and let $HK$ be perpendicular to $AB$, and cut $EF$ at $C$.**  $HK$ is $\perp$ to $EF$.  **Proof.** Suppose $MN$ drawn through $C \perp$ to $HK$.  $MN$ is $\parallel$ to $AB$.   $EF$ is $\parallel$ to $AB$.  $\therefore EF$ coincides with $MN$.  $MN$ is $\perp$ to $HK$.   $\therefore EF$ is $\perp$ to $HK$,   $HK$ is $\perp$ to $EF$.  ◻
**.** Def. A straight line that cuts two or more straight lines is called a **transversal** of those lines. ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/034bb109.png)
If the transversal $EF$ cuts $AB$ and $CD$, the angles $a$, $d$, $g$, $f$ are called *interior*angles; $b$, $c$, $h$, $e$ are called *exterior*angles. The angles $d$ and $f$, and $a$ and $g$, are called *alternate-interior*angles; the angles $b$ and $h$, and $c$ and $e$, are called *alternate-exterior*angles. The angles $b$ and $f$, $c$ and $g$, $e$ and $a$, $h$ and $d$, are called *exterior-interior*angles.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, the alternate-interior angles are equal.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/035aa110.png) **Let $EF$ and $GH$ be two parallel lines cut by the transversal $BC$.**  $\angle EBC$ $= \angle BCH$.  **Proof.** Through $O$, the middle point of $BC$, suppose $AD$ drawn $\perp$ to $GH$. $AD$ is likewise $\perp$ to $EF$, *(a straight line $\perp$ to one of two $\parallel_s$ is $\perp$ to the other),* $CD$ and $BA$ are both $\perp$ to $AD$. Apply the figure $COD$ to the figure $BOA$, so that $OD$ shall fall along $OA$. $OC$ will fall along $OB$, *(since $\angle COD = \angle BOA$, being vertical $\angle_s$);* $C$ will fall on $B$, *(since $OC = OB$, by construction).* the $\perp CD$ will fall along the $\perp BA$, *(only one $\perp$ can be drawn to a given line from a given external point).* $\therefore \angle OCD$ coincides with $\angle OBA$, and is equal to it, *(two angles are equal, if their vertices coincide and their sides coincide, each with each).* q.e.d. ◻
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *Conversely: When two straight lines in the same plane are cut by a transversal, if the alternate-interior angles are equal, the two straight lines are parallel.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/036aa111.png) **Let $EF$ cut the straight lines $AB$ and $CD$ in the points $H$ and $K$, and let the angles $AHK$ and $HKD$ be equal.**  $AB$ is $\parallel$ to $CD$.  **Proof**. Suppose $MN$ drawn through $H \parallel$ to $CD$.  $\angle MHK$ $= \angle HKD$,  *(being alt.-int. $\angle_s$ of $\parallel$ lines).*  $\angle AHK$ $= \angle HKD$.   $\therefore \angle MHK$ $= \angle AHK$.  $\therefore MN$ and $AB$ coincide.  $MN$ is $\parallel$ to $CD$.  $\therefore AB$, which coincides with $MN$, is $\parallel$ to $CD$. ◻
**Ex. **.** ** Find the complement and the supplement of an angle that contains $37°\ 53'\ 49''$. **Ex. **.** ** If the complement of an angle is one third of its supplement, how many degrees does the angle contain? Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, the exterior-interior angles are equal.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/037aa112.png) **Let $AB$ and $CD$ be two parallel lines cut by the transversal $EF$, in the points $H$ and $K$.**  $\angle EHB$ $= \angle HKD$.   $\angle EHB$ $= \angle AHK$,  *(being vertical $\angle_s$).*  $\angle AHK$ $= \angle HKD$,  *(being alt.-int. $\angle_s$ of $\parallel$ lines).*  $\therefore \angle EHB$ $= \angle HKD$.   $\angle EHA$ $= \angle HKC$.  ◻
**.** Cor. 
The alternate-exterior angles $EHB$ and $CKF$, and also $AHE$ and $DKF$, are equal.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Conversely: When two straight lines in a plane are cut by a transversal, if the exterior-interior angles are equal, these two straight lines are parallel.* (Proof similar to that in § 111.)
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, the two interior angles on the same side of the transversal are supplementary.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/038aa115.png) **Let $AB$ and $CD$ be two parallel lines cut by the transversal $EF$ in the points $H$ and $K$.** *To prove that $\angle_s BHK$ and $HKD$ are supplementary.* $\angle EHB + \angle BHK = \text{a st.\ }\angle$, *(being sup.-adj. $\angle_s$).* $\angle EHB = \angle HKD$, *(being ext.-int. $\angle_s$ of $\parallel$ lines).* $\therefore \angle BHK + \angle HKD = \text{a st.\ }\angle$. $\therefore \angle_s BHK$ and $HKD$ are supplementary. q.e.d. ◻
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *Conversely: When two straight lines in a plane are cut by a transversal, if two interior angles on the same side of the transversal are supplementary, the two straight lines are parallel.* (Proof similar to that in § 111.) ◻
## TRIANGLES.
A **triangle** is a portion of a plane bounded by three straight lines; as, $ABC$ (Fig. 1). ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/039aa117.png)![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/039bb118.png) The bounding lines are called the **sides**of the triangle, and their sum is called its **perimeter**; the angles included by the sides are called the **angles** of the triangle, and the vertices of these angles, the **vertices** of the triangle.
**Adjacent angles**of a rectilinear figure are two angles that have one side of the figure common; as, angles $A$ and $B$ (Fig. 2).
An **exterior angle** of a triangleis an angle included by one side and another side produced; as, $ACD$ (Fig. 2). The interior angle $ACB$ is adjacent to the exterior angle; the interior angles, $A$ and $B$, are called **opposite interior angles**.
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/039ce119.png)
A triangle is called a **scalene triangle** when no two of its sides are equal; an **isosceles triangle**, when two of its sides are equal; an **equilateral triangle**, when its three sides are equal. ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/039fi120.png)
A triangle is called a **right triangle**, when one of its angles is a right angle; an **obtuse triangle**, when one of its angles is an obtuse angle; an **acute triangle**, when all three of its angles are acute angles; an **equiangular triangle**, when its three angles are equal.
In a right triangle, the side opposite the right angle is called the **hypotenuse**, and the other two sides the **legs**.
The side on which a triangle is supposed to stand is called the baseof the triangle. In the isosceles triangle, the equal sides are called the legs, and the other side, the base; in other triangles, any one of the sides may be taken as the base.
The angle opposite the base of a triangle is called the **vertical angle**, and its vertex, the **vertex** of the triangle.
The **altitude** of a triangleis the perpendicular from the vertex to the base, or to the base produced; as, $AD$ (Fig. 1).
The three perpendiculars from the vertices of a triangle to the opposite sides (produced if necessary) are called the **altitudes** of the triangle; the three bisectors of the angles are called the **bisectors** of the triangle; and the three lines from the vertices to the middle points of the opposite sides are called the **medians**of the triangle.
If two triangles have the angles of the one equal, respectively, to the angles of the other, the equal angles are called **homologous angles**, and the sides opposite the equal angles are called **homologous sides**.
Two triangles are equal in all respects if they can be made to coincide (§ 60). The homologous sides of *equal triangles* are equal, and the homologous angles are equal.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *The sum of the three angles of a triangle is equal to two right angles.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/041aa129.png) **Let $A$, $B$, and $BCA$ be the angles of the triangle $ABC$.** *To prove that $\angle A+\angle B+\angle BCA = 2$ rt. $\angle_s$.* **Proof.** Suppose $CE$ drawn $\parallel$ to $AS$, and prolong $AC$ to $F$. $\angle ECF + \angle ECB + \angle BCA = 2$ rt. $\angle_s$, *(the sum of all the $\angle_s$ about a point on the same side of a straight line passing through the point is equal to $2$ rt. $\angle_s$).*  $\angle A$ $= \angle ECF$,  *(being ext.-int. $\angle_s$ of the $\parallel$ lines $AB$ and $CE$),*  $\angle B$ $= \angle BCE$,  *(being alt.-int. $\angle_s$ of the $\parallel$ lines $AB$ and $CE$).* Put for the $\angle_s ECF$ and $BCE$ their equals, the $\angle_s A$ and $B$. $\angle A +\angle B + \angle BCA = 2$ rt. $\angle_s$. ◻
**.** Cor. 1. 
The sum of two angles of a triangle is less than two right angles.
**.** Cor. 2. 
If the sum of two angles of a triangle is taken from two right angles, the remainder is equal to the third angle.
**.** Cor. 3. 
If two triangles have two angles of the one equal to two angles of the other, the third angles are equal.
**.** Cor. 4. 
If two right triangles have an acute angle of the one equal to an acute angle of the other, the other acute angles are equal.
**.** Cor. 5. 
In a triangle there can be but one right angle, or one obtuse angle.
**.** Cor. 6. 
In a right triangle the two acute angles are together equal to one right angle, or $90°$.
**.** Cor. 7. 
In an equiangular triangle, each angle is one third of two right angles, or $60°$.
**.** Cor. 8. 
An exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the two opposite interior angles, and therefore greater than either of them.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *The sum of two sides of a triangle is greater than the third side, and their difference is less than the third side.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/042aa138.png) **In the triangle $ABC$, let $AC$ be the longest side.** *To prove that $AB + BC > AC$, and $AC - BC < AB$*. $AB + BC > AC$, *(a straight line is the shortest line from one point to another).* Take away $BC$ from both sides. $AB > AC - BC$, $AC - BC < AB$. ◻
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *Two triangles are equal if two angles and the included side of the one are equal, respectively, to two angles and the included side of the other.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/043ab139.png) **In the triangles $ABC$, $DEF$, let the angle $A$ be equal to the angle $D$, $B$ to $E$, and the side $AB$ to $DE$.**  $\triangle ABC$ $= \triangle DEF$.  **Proof.** Apply the $\triangle ABC$ to the $\triangle DEF$ so that $AB$ shall coincide with its equal, $DE$. $AC$ will fall along $DF$, and $BC$ along $EF$, *(for $\angle A = \angle D$, and $\angle B = \angle E$, by hyp.).* $\therefore C$ will fall on $F$, *(two straight lines can intersect in only one point).* $\therefore$ the two $\triangle_s$ coincide, and are equal. q.e.d. ◻
**.** Cor. 1. 
Two triangles are equal if a side and any two angles of the one are equal to the homologous side and two angles of the other.
 § 132 **.** Cor. 2. 
Two right triangles are equal if the hypotenuse and an acute angle of the one are equal, respectively, to the hypotenuse and an acute angle of the other.
 § 133 **.** Cor. 3. 
Two right triangles are equal if a leg and an acute angle of the one are equal, respectively, to a leg and the homologous acute angle of the other.
 § 133 Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *Two triangles are equal if two sides and the included angle of the one are equal, respectively, to two sides and the included angle of the other.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/044ab143.png) **In the triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$, let $AB$ be equal to $DE$, $AC$ to $DF$, and the angle $A$ to the angle $D$.**  $\triangle ABC$ $= \triangle DEF$.  **Proof.** Apply the $\triangle ABC$ to the $\triangle DEF$ so that $AB$ shall coincide with its equal, $DE$. Then $AC$ will fall along $DF$, *(for $\angle A = \angle D$, by hyp.);* and $C$ will fall on $F$, *(for $AC = DF$, by hyp.).* $\therefore CB = FE$, *(their extremities being the same points).* $\therefore$ the two $\triangle_s$ coincide, and are equal. ◻
**.** Cor. 
Two right triangles are equal if their legs are equal, each to each.
Note. In § 139 we have given two angles and the included side, in § 143 two sides and the included angle; hence, by interchanging the words *sides* and *angles*, either theorem is changed to the other. This is called the *Principle of Duality*, or the *Principle of Reciprocity*. The reciprocal of a theorem is not always true, just as the converse of a theorem is not always true.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are equal.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/045aa145.png) **Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle, having $AB$ and $AC$ equal.**  $\angle B$ $= \angle C$.  **Proof.** Suppose $AD$ drawn so as to bisect the $\angle BAC$. In the $\triangle_s ADB$ and $ADC$,  $AB$ $=AC$,   $AD$ $=AD$,   and $\angle BAD$ $= \angle CAD$.   $\therefore \triangle ADB$ $= \triangle ADC$,  *(two $\triangle_s$ are equal if two sides and the included $\angle$ of the one are equal, respectively, to two sides and the included $\angle$ of the other).*  $\therefore \angle B$ $= \angle C$,  *(being homologous angles of equal triangles).* q.e.d. ◻
**.** Cor. 
An equilateral triangle is equiangular, and each angle is two thirds of a right angle.
**Ex. **.** ** If the equal sides of an isosceles triangle are produced, the angles on the other side of the base are equal. Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *If two angles of a triangle are equal, the sides opposite the equal angles are equal, and the triangle is isosceles.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/046aa147.png) **In the triangle $ABC$, let the angle $B$ be equal to the angle $C$.**  $AB$ $= AC$.  Suppose $AD$ drawn $\perp$ to $BC$. In the rt. $\triangle_s ADB$ and $ADC$,  $AD$ $= AD$,   and $\angle B$ $= \angle C$.   $\therefore$ rt. $\triangle ADB$ $=$ rt. $\triangle ADC$,  *(having a leg and an acute $\angle$ of the one equal, respectively, to a leg and the homologous acute $\angle$ of the other).*  $\therefore AB$ $= AC$,  *(being homologous sides of equal $\triangle_s$).* q.e.d. ◻
**.** Cor. 1. 
An equiangular triangle is also equilateral.
**.** Cor. 2. 
The perpendicular from the vertex to the base of an isosceles triangle bisects the base, and bisects the vertical angle of the triangle.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *Two triangles are equal if the three sides of the one are equal, respectively, to the three sides of the other.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/047ab150.png) **In the triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$, let $AB$ be equal to $A'B'$, $AC$ to $A'C'$, $BC$ to $B'C'$.**  $\triangle ABC$ $= \triangle A'B'C'$.  **Proof.** Place $\triangle A'B'C'$ in the position $\triangle AB'C$ having its greatest side $\triangle A'C'$ in coincidence with its equal $\triangle AC$, and its vertex at $B'$, opposite $B$; and draw $BB'$.  $AB$ $=AB'$   $\angle ABB'$ $= \angle AB'B$  *(in an isosceles $\triangle$ the $\angle_s$ opposite the equal sides are equal).*  $CB$ $= CB'$,   $\angle CBB'$ $= \angle CB'B$.   $\therefore \angle ABB' + \angle CBB'$ $= \angle AB'B + \angle CB'B$.   $\angle ABC$ $= \angle AB'C$.   $\therefore \triangle ABC$ $= \triangle AB'C$,  *(two $\triangle_s$ are equal if two sides and the included $\angle$ of the one are equal, respectively, to two sides and the included $\angle$ of the other).*  $\therefore \triangle ABC$ $= \triangle A'B'C'$.  ◻
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *Two right triangles are equal if a leg and the hypotenuse of the one are equal, respectively, to a leg and the hypotenuse of the other.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/048ac151.png) **In the right triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$, let $AB$ be equal to $A'B'$, and $AC$ to $A'C'$.**  $\triangle ABC$ $= \triangle A'B'C'$.  **Proof.** Apply the $\triangle ABC$ to the $\triangle A'B'C'$, so that $AB$ shall coincide with $A'B'$, $A$ falling on $A'$, $B$ on $B'$, and $C$ and $C'$ on opposite sides of $A'B'$. $BC$ will fall along $C'B'$ produced, *(for $\angle ABC = \angle A'B'C'$, each being a rt. $\angle$.).*  $AC$ $= A'C'$,  the $\triangle A'CC'$ is an isosceles triangle.  $\therefore \angle C$ $= \angle C'$,  *($\angle_s$ opposite the equal sides of an isosceles $\triangle$ are equal).* $\therefore \triangle_s ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are equal, *(two right $\triangle_s$ are equal if they have the hypotenuse and an acute $\angle$ of, the one equal to the hypotenuse and an acute $\angle$ of the other).* q.e.d. ◻
**Ex. **.** ** How many degrees are there in each of the acute angles of an isosceles right triangle? Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *If two sides of a triangle are unequal, the angles opposite are unequal, and the greater angle is opposite the greater side.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/049aa152.png) **In the triangle $ACB$, let $AB$ be greater than $AC$.** *To prove that $\angle ACB$ is greater than $\angle B$.* On $AB$ take $AE$ equal to $AC$. Draw $EC$.  $\angle AEC$ $= \angle ACE$  *(being $\angle_s$ opposite equal sides).* $\angle AEC$ is greater than $\angle B$ *(an exterior $\angle$ of a $\triangle$ is greater than either opposite interior $\angle$),* $\angle ACB$ is greater than $\angle ACE$. Substitute for $\angle ACE$ its equal $\angle AEC$, $\angle ACB$ is greater than $\angle AEC$. Since $\angle AEC$ is greater than $\angle B$, and $\angle ACB$ is greater than $\angle AEC$, $\angle ACB$ is greater than $\angle B$. ◻
**Ex. **.** ** If any angle of an isosceles triangle is equal to two thirds of a right angle ($60°$), what is the value of each of the two remaining angles? **Ex. **.** ** One angle of a triangle is $34°$. Find the other angles, if one of them is twice the other. Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *Reciprocally: If two angles of a triangle are unequal, the sides opposite are unequal, and the greater side is opposite the greater angle.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/050aa153.png) **In the triangle $ACB$, let the angle $C$ be greater than the angle $B$.** *To prove that $AB > AC$.* Now $AB=AC$, or $< AC$, or $>AC$. But $AB$ is not equal to $AC$; for then the $\angle C$ would be equal to the $\angle B$, *(being $\angle_s$ opposite equal sides).* And $AB$ is not less than $AC$; for then the $\angle C$ would be less than the $\angle B$. Both these conclusions are contrary to the hypothesis that the $\angle C$ is greater than the $\angle B$. Hence, $AB$ cannot be equal to $AC$ or less than $AC$. $\therefore AB > AC$. ◻
**Ex. **.** ** If the vertical angle of an isosceles triangle is equal to $30°$, find the exterior angle included by a side and the base produced. **Ex. **.** ** If the vertical angle of an isosceles triangle is equal to $36°$, find the angle included by the bisectors of the base angles. Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *If two triangles have two sides of the one equal, respectively, to two sides of the other, but the included angle of the first triangle greater than the included angle of the second, then the third side of the first is greater than the third side of the second.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/051ac154.png) **In the triangles $ABC$ and $ABE$, let $AB$ be equal to $AB$, $BC$ to $BE$; but let the angle $ABC$ be greater than the angle $ABE$.**  $AC$ $> AE$.  **Proof.** Place the $\triangle_s$ so that $AB$ of the one shall fall on $AB$ of the other, and $BE$ within the $\angle ABC$. Suppose $BF$ drawn to bisect the $\angle EBC$, and draw $EF$. The $\triangle_s EBF$ and $CBF$ are equal. § 143  $BF$ $= BF$,   $BE$ $=BC$,   $\angle EBF$ $=\angle CBF$.   $\therefore EF$ $=FC$.   $AF+FE$ $> AE$.   $\therefore AF+FC$ $> AE$.   $\therefore AC$ $> AE$.  ◻
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *Conversely: If two sides of a triangle are equal, respectively, to two sides of another, but the third side of the first triangle is greater than the third side of the second, then the angle opposite the third side of the first triangle is greater than the angle opposite the third side of the second.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/052ab155.png) **In the triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$, let $AB$ be equal to $DE$, $AC$ to $DF$; but let $BC$ be greater than EF.** *To prove that the $\angle A$ is greater than the $\angle D$.* **Proof**. Now the $\angle A$ is equal to the $\angle D$, or less than the $\angle D$, or greater than the $\angle D$. But the $\angle A$ is not equal to the $\angle D$; for then the $\triangle ABC$ would be equal to the $\triangle DEF$, *(having two sides and the included $\angle$ of the one equal, respectively, to two sides and the included $\angle$ of the other),* and $BC$ would be equal to $EF$. And the $\angle A$ is not less than the $\angle D$, for then $BC$ would be less than $EF$. § 154 Both these conclusions are contrary to the hypothesis that $BC$ is greater than $EF$. Since the $\angle A$ is not equal to the $\angle D$ or less than the $\angle D$, the $\angle A$ is greater than the $\angle D$. ◻
## LOCI OF POINTS.
If it is required to find a point which shall fulfil a *single* geometric condition, the point may have an *unlimited number of positions*. If, however, all the points are in the same plane, the required point will be confined to a *particular line*, or *group of lines*. A point in a plane at a given distance from a fixed straight line of indefinite length in that plane, is evidently in one of two straight lines, so drawn as to be everywhere at the given distance from the fixed line, one on one side of the fixed line, and the other on the other side of it. A point in a plane equidistant from two parallel lines in that plane is evidently in a straight line drawn between the two given parallel lines and everywhere equidistant from them.
All points in a plane that satisfy a single geometrical condition lie, in general, in a line or group of lines; and this line or group of lines is called the **locus** of the points that satisfy the given condition.
To prove *completely* that a certain line is the locus of points that fulfil a given condition, it is necessary to prove 1\. *Any point in the line satisfies the given condition; and any point not in the line does not satisfy the given condition.* Or, to prove 2\. *Any point that satisfies the given condition lies in the line; and any point in the line satisfies the given condition*.
Note. The word *locus* (pronounced lo\'kus) is a Latin word that signifies *place*. The plural of locus is loci (pronounced lo\'si).
**.** Def. A line which bisects a given line and is perpendicular to it is called the **perpendicular bisector** of the line. Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *The perpendicular bisectorof a given line is the locus of points equidistant from the extremities of the line.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/054aa160.png) **Let $PR$ be the perpendicular bisector of the line $AB$, $O$ any point in $PR$, and $C$ any point not in $PR$.** Draw $OA$ and $OB$, $CA$ and $CB$. *To prove $OA$ and $OB$ equal, $CA$ and $CB$ unequal.*  **1.** $\triangle OPA$ $= \triangle OPB$,  for $PA = PB$ by hypothesis, and $OP$ is common, *(two right $\triangle_s$ are equal if their legs are equal, each to each).*  $\therefore OA$ $= OB$.  **2. **Since $C$ is not in the $\perp$, $CA$ or $CB$ will cut the $\perp$. Let $CA$ cut the $\perp$ at $D$, and draw $DB$. Then, by the first part of the proof $DA = DB$. $CB < CD + DB$. $\therefore CB < CD + DA$. $CB < CA$. $\therefore PR$ is the locus of points equidistant from $A$ and $B$. § 158,1 q.e.d. ◻
**.** Cor. 
Two points each equidistant from the extremities of a line determine the perpendicular bisector of the line.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *The bisector of a given angle is the locus of points equidistant from the sides of the angle.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/055aa162.png) **Let $O$ be any point equidistant from the sides of the angle $PAQ$.** *To prove that $O$ is in the bisector of the $\angle PAQ$.* Draw $AO$. Suppose $OF$ drawn $\perp$ to $AP$ and $OG \perp$ to $AQ$. In the rt. $\triangle_s AFO$ and $AGO$,  $AO$ $= AO$,   $OF$ $= OG$,   $\therefore \triangle AFO$ $= \triangle AGO$.   $\therefore \angle FAO$ $= \angle GAO$.  $\therefore O$ is in the bisector of the $\angle PAQ$. **Let $\mathbf{D}$ be any point in the bisector of the angle $\mathbf{PAQ}$.** *To prove that $D$ is equidistant from $AP$ and $AQ$.* Suppose $DB$ drawn $\perp$ to $AP$ and $DC \perp$ to $AQ$. In the rt. $\triangle_s ABD$ and $ACD$,  $AD$ $= AD$,   $\angle DAB$ $= \angle DAC$,   $\therefore \triangle ABD$ $= \triangle ACD$.   $\therefore DB$ $= DC$.  $\therefore D$ is equidistant from $AP$ and $AQ$. $\therefore$ the bisector of the $\angle PAQ$ is the locus of points that are equidistant from its sides. ◻
## QUADRILATERALS.
A **quadrilateral** is a portion of a plane bounded by four straight lines. The bounding lines are the **sides**, the angles formed by these sides are the **angles**, and the vertices of these angles are the **vertices**, of the quadrilateral.
A **trapezium** is a quadrilateral which has no two sides parallel.
A **trapezoid** is a quadrilateral which has two sides, and only two sides, parallel.
A **parallelogram** is a quadrilateral which has its opposite sides parallel.
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/056ac166.png)
A **rectangle** is a parallelogram which has its angles right angles.
A **square** is a rectangle which has its sides equal.
A **rhomboid** is a parallelogram which has its angles oblique angles.
A **rhombus** is a rhomboid which has its sides equal.
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/056dg170.png)
The side upon which a parallelogram stands, and the opposite side, are called its lower and upper *bases*.
Two parallel sides of a trapezoid are called its **bases**, the other two sides its **legs**, and the line joining the middle points of the legs is called the **median** of the trapezoid.
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/057aa174.png)
A trapezoid is called an **isosceles trapezoid** if its legs are equal.
The **altitude** of a parallelogramor trapezoidis the perpendicular distance between its bases, as $PQ$.
A **diagonal**of a quadrilateral is a straight line joining two opposite vertices, as $AC$.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *Two angles whose sides are parallel, each to each, are either equal or supplementary.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/057bb176.png) **Let $BA$ be parallel to $HD$, and $BC$ be parallel to $MN$.** *To prove $\angle_s a$, $a'$ and $c$ equal; $a$ and $c'$ supplementary.* Let $HD$ and $BC$ prolonged intersect at $x$. $\angle a = \angle x$, and $\angle a' = \angle x$. $\therefore \angle a = \angle a'$. $\angle c = \angle a'$ (§ 93). $\therefore \angle c = \angle a$. $\angle a'$ and $\angle c'$ are supplementary. Put $\angle a$ for its equal, $\angle a'$. $\angle a$ and $\angle c'$ are supplementary. ◻
**.** Cor. 
The opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, and the adjacent angles are supplementary.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *The opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/058aa178.png) **Let the figure $ABCE$ be a parallelogram.** *To prove $BC = AE$, and $AB = EC$.* Draw the diagonal $AC$. $\triangle ABC = \triangle CEA$. For $AC$ is common, $\angle BAC = \angle ACE$, and $\angle ACB = \angle CAE$, *(being alt-int. $\angle_s$ of $\parallel$ lines).* $\therefore BC = AE$, and $AB = CE$, *(being homologous sides of equal $\triangle_s$).* q.e.d. ◻
**.** Cor. 1. 
A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two equal triangles.
**.** Cor. 2. 
Parallel lines comprehended between parallel lines are equal.
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/058bb181.png)
Cor. 3. 
Two parallel lines are everywhere equally distant.
For if $AB$ and $DC$ are parallel, $\perp_s$ dropped from *any* points in $AB$ to $DC$, are equal, § 180. Hence, *all* points in $AB$ are equidistant from $DC$.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *If the opposite sides of a quadrilateral are equal, the figure is a parallelogram.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/059aa182.png) **Let the figure $ABCE$ be a quadrilateral, having $BC$ equal to $AE$ and $AB$ to $EC$.** *To prove that the figure $ABCE$ is a $\Par$.* Draw the diagonal $AC$. In the $\triangle_s ABC$ and $CEA$,  $BC$ $= AE$,   $AB$ $= CE$,   $AC$ $= AC$,   $\therefore \triangle ABC$ $= \triangle CEA$,  *(having three sides of the one equal, respectively, to the three sides of the other).*  $\therefore \angle ACB$ $= \angle CAE$,   $\angle BAC$ $= \angle ACE$,  *(being homologous $\angle_s$ of equal $\triangle_s$).*  $\therefore BC$ is $\parallel$ to $AE$,   $AB$ is $\parallel$ to $EC$,  *(two lines in the same plane cut by a transversal are parallel, if the alt.-int. $\angle_s$ are equal).* $\therefore$ the figure $ACBE$ is a $\Par$, *(having its opposite sides parallel).* ◻
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *If two sides of a quadrilateral are equal and parallel, then the other two sides are equal and parallel, and the figure is a parallelogram.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/060aa183.png) **Let the figure $ABCE$ be a quadrilateral, having the side $AE$ equal and parallel to $BC$.** *To prove that $AB$ is equal and parallel to $EC$.* Draw $AC$. The $\triangle_s ABC$ and $CEA$ are equal, § 143 *(having two sides and the included $\angle$ of each equal, respectively).* $AC$ is common,  $BC$ $=AE$   $\angle BCA$ $= \angle CAE$,  *(being alt.-int. $\angle_s$ of $\parallel$ lines).*  $\therefore AB$ $=EC$,   $\angle BAC$ $= \angle ACE$,  *(being homologous parts of equal $\triangle_s$).* $\therefore AB$ is $\parallel$ to $EC$, *(two lines are $\parallel$, if the alt.-int. $\angle_s$ are equal).* $\therefore$ the figure $ABCE$ is a $\Par$, *(the opposite sides being parallel).* q.e.d. ◻
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/061aa184.png) **Let the figure $ABCE$ be a parallelogram, and let the diagonals $AC$ and $BE$ cut each other at $O$.** *To prove that $AO = OC$, and $BO = OE$.* **Proof.** In the $\triangle_s AOE$ and $COB$,  $AE$ $=BC$,  *(being opposite sides of a $\Par$).*  $\angle OAE$ $=\angle OCB$,   and $\angle OEA$ $= \angle OBC$,  *(being alt.-int. $\angle_s$ of $\parallel$ lines).*  $\therefore\triangle AOE$ $=\triangle COB$,  *(having two $\angle_s$ and the included side of the one equal, respectively, to two $\angle_s$ and the included side of the other).* $\therefore AO=OC$, and $BO=OE$, *(being homologous sides of equal $\triangle_s$).* q.e.d. ◻
**Ex. **.** ** The median from the vertex to the base of an isosceles triangle is perpendicular to the base, and bisects the vertical angle. **Ex. **.** ** If two straight lines are cut by a transversal so that the alternate-exterior angles are equal, the two straight lines are parallel. **Ex. **.** ** If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, the two exterior angles on the same side of the transversal are supplementary. **Ex. **.** ** If two straight lines are cut by a transversal so as to make the exterior angles on the same side of the transversal supplementary, the two lines are parallel. Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *Two parallelograms are equal, if two sides and the included angle of the one are equal, respectively, to two sides and the included angle of the other.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/062ab185.png) **In the parallelograms $ABCD$ and $A'B'C'D'$, let $AB$ be equal to $A'B'$, $AD$ to $A'D'$, and angle $A$ to $A'$.** *To prove that the $\Par_s$ are equal*. **Proof.** Place the $\Par$ $ABCD$ on the $\Par$ $A'B'C'D'$, so that $AD$ will fall on and coincide with its equal, $A'D'$. Then $AB$ will fall on $A'B'$, and $B$ on $B'$; *(for $\angle A = \angle A'$, and $AB = A'B'$, by hyp.)* Now, $BC$ and $B'C'$ are both $\parallel$ to $A'D'$ and drawn through $B'$. $\therefore BC$ and $B'C'$ coincide, *(through a given point only one line can be drawn $\parallel$ to a given line).* Also $DC$ and $D'C'$ are $\parallel$ to $A'B'$ and drawn through $D'$. $\therefore DC$ and $D'C'$ coincide. $\therefore C$ falls on $C'$, *(two lines can intersect in only one point),* $\therefore$ the two $\Par_s$ coincide, and are equal. ◻
**.** Cor. 
Two rectangles having equal bases and altitudes are equal.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *If three or more parallels intercept equal parts on one transversal, they intercept equal parts on every transversal.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/063aa187.png) **Let the parallels $AH$, $BK$, $CM$, $DP$ intercept equal parts $HK$, $KM$, $MP$ on the transversal $HP$.** *To prove that they intercept equal parts $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ on the transversal $AD$.* **Proof.** Suppose $AH$, $BF$, and $CG$ drawn $\parallel$ to $HP$. $\angle_s$ $AEB$, $BFC$, etc. $=\angle_s$ $HKE$, $KMF$, etc., respectively. But $\angle_s$ $HKE$, $KMF$, etc. are equal. $\therefore \angle_s$ $AEB$, $BFC$, etc. are equal. Also $\angle_s$ $BAE$, $CBF$, etc. are equal. Now $AE = HK$, $BF = KM$, $CG = MP$, *(parallels comprehended between parallels are equal).* $\therefore AE = BF = CG$. $\therefore \triangle ABE = \triangle BCF = \triangle CDG$, *(having two $\angle_s$ and the included side of each respectively equal).* $\therefore AB = BC = CD$. q.e.d. ◻
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/064aa188.png)
Cor. 1. 
If a line is parallel to the base of a triangle and bisects one side, it bisects the other side also.
Let $DE$ be $\parallel$ to $BC$ and bisect $AB$. Suppose a line is drawn through $A \parallel$ to $BC$. Then this line is $\parallel$ to $DE$, by § 106. The three parallels by hypothesis intercept equal parts on the transversal $AB$, and therefore, by § 187, they intercept equal parts on the transversal $AC$; that is, the line $DE$ bisects $AC$.
Cor. 2. 
The line which joins the middle points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side, and is equal to half the third side.
A line drawn through $D$, the middle point of $AB$, $\parallel$ to $BC$, passes through $E$, the middle point of $AC$, by § 188. Therefore the line joining $D$ and $E$ coincides with this parallel and is $\parallel$ to $BC$. Also, since $EF$ drawn $\parallel$ to $AB$ bisects $AC$, it bisects $BC$, by § 188; that is, $BF=FC = \frac{1}{2}BC$. But $BDEF$ is a $\Par$ by § 166, and therefore $DE = BF = \frac{1}{2}BC$.
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/064bb190.png)
Cor. 3. 
The median of a trapezoid is parallel to the bases, and is equal to half the sum of the bases.
Draw the diagonal $DB$. In the $\triangle ADB$ join $E$, the middle point of $AD$, to $F$, the middle point of $DB$. Then, by § 189, $EF$ is $\parallel$ to $AB$ and $= \frac{1}{2}AB$. In the $\triangle DBC$ join $F$ to $G$, the middle point of $BC$. Then $FG$ is $\parallel$ to $DC$ and $=\frac{1}{2}DC$. $AB$ and $FG$, being $\parallel$ to $DC$, are $\parallel$ to each other. But only one line can be drawn through $F \parallel$ to $AB$ (§ 105). Therefore $FG$ is the prolongation of $EF$. Hence, $EFG$ is parallel to $AB$ and $DC$, and equal to $\frac{1}{2} (AB + DC)$.
## POLYGONS IN GENERAL.
A **polygon** is a portion of a plane bounded by straight lines. The bounding lines are the sides, and their sum, the **perimeter**of the polygon. The angles included by the adjacent sides are the **angles**of the polygon, and the vertices of these angles are the **vertices** of the polygon. The number of sides of a polygon is evidently equal to the number of its angles.
A **diagonal**of a polygon is a line joining the vertices of two angles not adjacent; as, $AC$ (Fig. 1). ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/065ac192.png)
An **equilateral polygon** is a polygon which has all its sides equal.
An **equiangular polygon** is a polygon which has all its angles equal.
A **convex polygon** is a polygon of which no side, when produced, will enter the polygon.
A **concave polygon** is a polygon of which two or more sides, if produced, will enter the polygon.
Each angle of a convex polygon (Fig. 2) is called a *salient*angle, and is less than a straight angle.
The angle $EDF$ of the concave polygon (Fig. 3) is called a *re-entrant* angle, and is greater than a straight angle. When the term polygon is used, a *convex* polygon is meant.
Two polygons are *equal* when they can be divided by diagonals into the same number of triangles, equal each to each, and similarly placed; for if the polygons are applied to each other, the corresponding triangles will coincide, and hence the polygons will coincide and be equal.
Two polygons are *mutually equiangular*, if the angles of the one are equal to the angles of the other, each to each, when taken in the same order. Figs. 1 and 2.
The equal angles in mutually equiangular polygons are called *homologous* angles; and the sides which are included by homologous angles are called *homologous* sides.
Two polygons are *mutually equilateral*, if the sides of the one are equal to the sides of the other, each to each, when taken in the same order. Figs. 1 and 2. ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/066ad203.png)
Two polygons may be mutually equiangular without being mutually equilateral; as, Figs. 4 and 5. And, *except in the case of triangles*, two polygons may be mutually equilateral without being mutually equiangular; as, Figs. 6 and 7. If two polygons are mutually equilateral and mutually equiangular *they are equal*, for they can be made to coincide.
A polygon of three sides is called a *triangle*; one of four sides, a *quadrilateral*; one of five sides, a *pentagon*; one of six sides, a *hexagon*; one of seven sides, a *heptagon*; one of eight sides, an *octagon*; one of ten sides, a *decagon*; one of twelve sides, a *dodecagon*.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *The sum of the interior angles of a polygon is equal to two right angles, taken as many times less two as the figure has sides.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/067aa205.png) **Let the figure $ABCDEF$ be a polygon, having $n$ sides.** *To prove that $\angle A + \angle B + \angle C$, etc. $= (n-2)2$ rt. $\angle_s$.* **Proof.** From $A$ draw the diagonals $AC$, $AD$, and $AE$. The sum of the $\angle_s$ of the $\triangle_s$ is equal to the sum of the $\angle_s$ of the polygon. Now, there are $(n-2)$ $\triangle_s$, and the sum of the $\angle_s$ of each $\triangle = 2$ rt. $\angle_s$. $\therefore$ the sum of the $\angle_s$ of the $\triangle_s$, that is, the sum of the $\angle_s$ of the polygon is equal to $(n-2) 2$ rt. $\triangle_s$. q.e.d. ◻
**.** Cor. 
The sum of the angles of a quadrilateral equals 4 right angles; and if the angles are all equal, each is a right angle. In general, each angle of an equiangular polygon of $n$ sides is equal to $\displaystyle \frac{2(n-2)}{n}$ right angles.
**Ex. **.** ** How many diagonals can be drawn in a polygon of $n$ sides? Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *The exterior angles of a polygon, made by producing each of its sides in succession, are together equal to four right angles.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/068aa207.png) **Let the figure $ABCDE$ be a polygon, having its sides produced in succession.** *To prove the sum of the ext. $\angle_s = 4$ rt. $\angle_s$.* **Proof.** Denote the int. $\angle_s$ of the polygon by $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, and the corresponding ext. $\angle_s$ by $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $e$.  $\angle A + \angle a$ $= 2$ rt. $\angle_s$,   $\angle B + \angle b$ $= 2$ rt. $\angle_s$,  *(being sup.-adj. $\angle_s$).* In like manner each pair of adj. $\angle_s = 2$ rt. $\angle_s$. $\therefore$ the sum of the interior and exterior $\angle_s$ of a polygon of $n$ sides is equal to $2n$ rt. $\angle_s$. But the sum of the interior $\angle_s = (n-2) 2$ rt. $\angle_s$§ 205\ $\phantom{\text{ But the sum of the interior}~\angle_s} = 2 n$ rt. $\angle_s - 4$ rt. $\angle_s$. $\therefore$ the sum of the exterior $\angle_s = 4$ rt. $\angle_s$. ◻
**Ex. **.** ** How many sides has a polygon if the sum of its interior $\angle_s$ is twice the sum of its exterior $\angle_s$? ten times the sum of its exterior $\angle_s$? ## SYMMETRY.
Two points are said to be **symmetrical** with respect to a third point, called the **centre of symmetry**, if this third point bisects the straight line which joins them. ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/069ac208.png) Two points are said to be *symmetrical* with respect to a straight line, called the **axis of symmetry**, if this straight line bisects at right angles the straight line which joins them. Thus, $P$ and $P'$ are symmetrical with respect to $O$ as a centre, and $XX'$ as an axis, if $O$ bisects the line $PP'$, and if $XX'$ bisects $PP'$ at right angles.
A figure is symmetrical with respect to a point as a centre of symmetry, if the point bisects every straight line drawn through it and terminated by the boundary of the figure.
A figure is symmetrical with respect to a line as an axis of symmetry if one of the parts of the figure coincides, point for point, with the other part when it is folded over on that line as an axis.
![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/069dd211.png)
Two figures are said to be symmetrical with respect to an axis if every point of one has a corresponding symmetrical point in the other. Thus, if every point in the figure $A'B'C'$ has a symmetrical point in $ABC$, with respect to $XX'$ as an axis, the figure $A'B'C'$ is symmetrical to $ABC$ with respect to $XX'$ as an axis.
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *A quadrilateral which has two adjacent sides equal, and the other two sides equal, is symmetrical with respect to the diagonal joining the vertices of the angles formed by the equal sides, and the diagonals are perpendicular to each other.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/070aa212.png) **Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral, having $AB$ equal to $AD$, and $CB$ equal to $CD$, and having the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$.** *To prove that the diagonal $AC$ is an axis of symmetry, and that it is $\perp$ to the diagonal $BD$.* **Proof.** In the $\triangle_s ABC$ and $ADC$, $AB = AD$, and $BC = DC$,  $AC$ $= AC$.   $\therefore \triangle ABC$ $= \triangle ADC$.  $\therefore \angle BAC = \angle DAC$, and $\angle BCA = \angle DCA$. Hence, if $ABC$ is turned on $AC$ as an axis until it falls on $ADC$, $AB$ will fall upon $AD$, $CB$ on $CD$, and $OB$ on $OD$. $\therefore$ the $\triangle ABC$ will coincide with the $\triangle ADC$. $\therefore AC$ is an axis of symmetry (§ 210) and is $\perp$ to $BD$. q.e.d. ◻
Proposition . Theorem.
*Proof.* *If a figure is symmetrical with respect to two axes perpendicular to each other, it is symmetrical with respect to their intersection as a centre.* ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/071aa213.png) **Let the figure $ABCDEFGH$ be symmetrical with respect to the two perpendicular axes $XX'$, $YY'$, which intersect at $O$.** *To prove that $O$ is the centre of symmetry of the figure.* **Proof.** Let $N$ be any point in the perimeter. Suppose $NMI$ drawn $\perp$ to $YY'$, $IKL \perp$ to $XX'$. $NI$ is $\parallel$ to $XX'$ and $IL$ is $\parallel$ to $YY'$. Draw $LO$, $ON$, and $KM$.  $KI$ $= KL$,  *(the figure being symmetrical with respect to $XX'$).*  $KI$ $=OM$.  $\therefore KL=OM$, and $KLOM$ is a $\Par$. $\therefore LO$ is equal and parallel to $KM$. In like manner $ON$ is equal and parallel to $KM$. $\therefore LON$ is a straight line. $\therefore O$ bisects $LN$, *any* straight line and therefore *every* straight line drawn through $O$ and terminated by the perimeter. $\therefore O$ is the centre of symmetry of the figure. ◻
### REVIEW QUESTIONS ON BOOK I.
What is the subject-matter of Geometry? What is a geometric magnitude? What is an axiom? a theorem? a converse theorem? an opposite theorem? a contradictory theorem? Define a straight line; a curved line; a broken line; a plane surface; a curved surface. How many points are necessary to determine a straight line? How many straight lines are necessary to determine a point? On what does the magnitude of an angle depend? Define a straight angle; a right angle; an oblique angle. Define adjacent angles; complementary angles; supplementary angles; conjugate angles. Define parallel lines and give the axiom of parallels. If two lines in the same plane are parallel and cut by a transversal, what pairs of angles are equal? what pairs are supplementary? Define a right triangle; an isosceles triangle; a scalene triangle. To how many right angles is the sum of the angles of a triangle equal? the sum of the acute angles of a right triangle? To what angles is the exterior angle of a triangle equal? What is the test of equality of two geometric magnitudes? How does a reciprocal theorem differ from a converse theorem? State the three cases in which two triangles are equal. State the cases in which two right triangles are equal. What is meant by a locus of points? Where are the points located in a plane that are each equidistant from two given points? from two intersecting lines? Define a parallelogram; a trapezoid; an isosceles trapezoid. When is a figure symmetrical with respect to a centre? When is a figure symmetrical with respect to an axis? Must a triangle be equiangular if equilateral? must a triangle be equilateral if equiangular? When are two polygons said to be mutually equiangular? When are two polygons said to be mutually equilateral? Can two polygons of more than three sides be mutually equiangular without being mutually equilateral? mutually equilateral without being mutually equiangular? What line do two points each equidistant from the extremities of a given straight line determine?
### METHODS OF PROVING THEOREMS.
There are *three* general methods of proving theorems, the **synthetic**, the **analytic**, and the **indirect** methods. The *synthetic* method is the method employed in most of the theorems already given, and consists in putting together known truths in order to obtain a new truth. The *analytic* method is the reverse of the synthetic method. It asserts that the conclusion is true if another proposition is true, and so on step by step, until a known truth is reached. Thus, proposition $A$ is true if proposition $B$ is true, and $B$ is true if $C$ is true; but $C$ *is* true, hence $A$ and $B$ are true. If a known truth *suggests* the required proof, it is best to use the synthetic form at once. If no proof occurs to the mind, it is necessary to use the analytic method to *discover* the proof, and then the synthetic proof may be given. The *indirect* method, or the method of *reductio ad absurdum*, is illustrated on page . It consists in proving a theorem to be true by proving its contradictory to be false.
Generally auxiliary lines are required, as a line *connecting two points*; a line *parallel to or perpendicular to a given line*; a line *produced by its own length*; a line *making with another line an angle equal to a given angle.* **Two lines are proved equal** by proving them *homologous sides of equal triangles*; or *legs of an isosceles triangle*; or *opposite sides of a parallelogram.* **Two angles are proved equal** by proving them *alternate-interior angles or exterior-interior angles of parallel lines*; or *homologous angles of equal triangles*; or *base angles of an isosceles triangle*; or *opposite angles of a parallelogram.* Two suggestions are of special importance to the beginner:
*Draw as accurate figures as possible.* *Draw as general figures as possible.*
## EXERCISES. Prove by the analytic method: ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/074aaZ19.png)
*A median of a triangle is less than half the sum of the two adjacent sides.* *To prove the median $AD < \frac{1}{2}(AB + AC)$.*   $AD < \frac{1}{2}(AB + AC)$,    $2AD < AB + AC$.  This suggests producing $AD$ by its own length to $E$, and joining $BE$.   $AE=2AD$,  $2AD ![image](images/wentworth-plane-geometry-1899/images/074bbZ20.png)
*A straight line which bisects two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side.* If $AD = DB$ and $AE = EC$, to prove $DE\parallel$ to $BC$. Draw $CG\parallel$ to $BA$, and produce $DE$ to meet it at $G$. $DE$ is $\parallel$ to $BC$ if $BCGD$ is a $\Par$. $BCGD$ is a $\Par$ if $CG=BD$. $CG=BD$ if each is equal to $AD$.  $BD$ $=AD$.   $CG$ $=AD$ if $\triangle CGE = \triangle ADE$.   $\triangle CGE$ $=\triangle ADE$.   $EC$ $=AE$.   $\angle GEC$ $=\angle AED$.   $\angle ECG$ $=\angle DAE$.  $\therefore DE$ is $\parallel$ to $BC$.
Prove by the synthetic method:
